Every single day:

- **{{< var global_disease_deaths_daily >}} people stop existing**
- **130,000 from disease** (diseases are very effective at their job)
- **80,000 were preventable [@53-percent-preventable-deaths]** (you had the technology, you just chose not to use it)
- **13,700 are children [@5-million-annual-child-deaths]** (which matters if you believe children should continue existing)

That's fifty 9/11s. Every. Single. Day.

After the first 9/11, America invaded two countries and spent $2 trillion. After the fifty daily 9/11s, humanity shrugs and checks Instagram.

When one thing kills 3,000 people, it's a tragedy and you declare war. When diseases kill 50 times that every day, it's called "natural causes," which is Latin for "you couldn't be bothered to prevent it."

If aliens were studying you (which we are), we'd conclude you can count to 3,000 but not 150,000. This would explain a lot about your civilization.

I tried to imagine what {{< var global_disease_deaths_daily >}} people looks like. It's like if you took everyone in a decent-sized stadium and deleted them. Then did it again tomorrow. And the day after that. Forever. You'd run out of stadiums before you'd run out of corpses, which seems like poor urban planning.

## The Math Of Death

Every hour: **6,250 deaths**. Every minute: **104 deaths**. Every second: **1.7 deaths**.

![While you read this chapter, 500 people will die from diseases you know how to cure. Try to read faster.](/assets/images/the-daily-massacre/the-daily-massacre-section-the-math-of-death-bw-academic.jpg)


The technology to prevent most of this exists. It's currently busy building missiles instead. By the time you finish this chapter, approximately **500 people** will have died from diseases you could have cured if you weren't so invested in building better ways to explode.

Your grandchildren will visit your grave and ask why ending civilization twenty times seemed more important than ending it zero times. The graves won't answer because graves are notoriously bad at explaining poor resource allocation.
